chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
title: Repertoire then and now: Berlin and Porter versus rock and roll
summary: Musicians once played more songs; today's repertoire has little place for the standards, and good songs went unknown without plugging.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: In a way, I guess it just occurred to me... I guess musicians used to play a lot more different tunes than today, because the repertoire, you know...for instance, say, on your gig now, it's relatively restricted, isn't it? I mean, there are not too many...
Well, yeah. Most of the songs now that they sing are sort of Rock-and-Roll; they're Rock-and-Roll songs, sorta like, you know, or mountain(?) songs.
So they don't adapt themselves to...
Yeah. You know, like, popular songs, like the kind that Berlin wrote and those people like that, Porter and all them... They don't use those songs. There is no place to put them in Rock-and-Roll.
So that's the way it goes. To me. To my estimation.

But for instance, say you were playing in a band in the Thirties, you'd have to change what you play every now and then, because they would be plugging some song, and your band would have made a record, and they would feature that, and so on. So there would more of a change, a variety in what you were playing. Although some of those songs, I guess, were played once or twice and then never again also.

Yes, that's right. And there were some beautiful songs that no one knew about, that were very good songs. But somebody got to get their songs plugged ahead of it, or had money enough to get it pushed.
